nameStory: The name 'butterbur' comes from the traditional use of this plant's enormous leaves to wrap butter and other foods for storage and transport. The leaves can grow as large as dinner plates, making them perfect natural wrappers in the days before refrigeration and plastic wrap.
description: Common Butterbur is a robust perennial herb that produces some of the largest leaves you'll find in New England's wild places. The plant sends up clusters of pinkish-white flowers in early spring before the massive, heart-shaped leaves appear. These leaves can grow over a foot wide, creating impressive ground-covering patches along streams and in wet areas. The whole plant grows from thick underground stems called rhizomes that spread to form colonies.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Enormous heart-shaped leaves that can reach 12-18 inches across, with a soft, fuzzy texture underneath and prominent veins radiating from the base like fingers on a hand

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Dense clusters of small pinkish-white flowers appear in early spring on thick, scaly stems before the leaves emerge, resembling chunky asparagus spears topped with bottle brushes

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms large colonies along waterways, with leaves emerging directly from the ground on long, thick leaf stalks that feel hollow and somewhat spongy when squeezed

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Flower stems are thick, fleshy, and covered with overlapping brownish scales that feel papery to the touch, while leaf stems are smooth and substantial

habitat: Look for Common Butterbur along stream banks, in wet meadows, and in other consistently moist areas throughout New England. It thrives in rich, organic soils and often forms large colonies in partially shaded spots near water sources. You'll frequently find it growing alongside skunk cabbage, marsh marigold, and other moisture-loving plants.

seasonality.spring: The most exciting time to spot butterbur, when chunky flower clusters emerge from the ground in March and April, followed by the dramatic unfurling of the giant leaves.
seasonality.summer: Massive leaves dominate the landscape, creating impressive green carpets along waterways that can completely hide the plant's flowers from earlier in the year.
seasonality.fall: Leaves begin to yellow and die back, revealing the extensive colony structure as the plant prepares for winter dormancy.
seasonality.winter: Plants die back completely to underground rhizomes, leaving only dead leaf stalks and the promise of next spring's dramatic emergence.

funFact: Common Butterbur is one of the few plants where male and female flowers grow on completely separate plants, and in North America, almost all butterbur colonies are female clones that rarely produce viable seeds - they spread almost entirely by their creeping underground stems!
confusionNotes: The massive leaves might be confused with those of wild rhubarb or large dock species, but butterbur's leaves are distinctly heart-shaped and have a soft, fuzzy underside. Remember: if the leaves are growing near water and feel velvety underneath, think butterbur.
contextualKnowledge: While butterbur has been used in traditional European medicine for centuries and is still sold as a dietary supplement, it contains compounds called pyrrolizidine alkaloids that can be toxic. This is definitely a 'look but don't taste' plant, despite its long history of human use.
compareHints: Common Butterbur is much smaller than its relative Giant Butterbur, whose leaves can reach 3 feet across. Arctic Butterbur, found in northern regions, has much smaller, more triangular leaves and grows in different habitats. If you see dinner-plate sized heart-shaped leaves by a stream, it's almost certainly Common Butterbur.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Giant Butterbur lives up to its name by being much larger than its relatives – Common Butterbur has similar but smaller leaves (usually under a foot wide), while Arctic Butterbur is tiny in comparison with leaves only a few inches across.
Arctic Butterbur is much smaller and more delicate than its relatives Giant Butterbur and Common Butterbur, with only 5-12 flower heads compared to their dozens or hundreds.
